name: Substation
whatItIs: A fenced electrical yard where high-voltage transmission power is stepped down to voltages the data center can use. Large campuses often have a dedicated substation built by the utility on or next to the site.
whyItExists: Data centers draw far more power than a normal commercial building, so they connect closer to the transmission system instead of the neighborhood distribution lines that serve homes.
communityImpact: Visual presence of steel structures and lines, a low steady transformer hum, and construction traffic while it is built. Who pays for it matters: costs can be assigned to the data center or spread across utility customers depending on the tariff.
mitigation: Setbacks and screening walls or vegetation (several Virginia counties now require substation screening), low-noise transformer specifications, and utility agreements that assign interconnection costs to the data center customer.
monitoring: Interconnection agreements and cost allocations are filed with state utility commissions and are public records. Residents can also ask for the sound study covering the substation at the property line.

name: Transformers
whatItIs: Devices that change electricity from one voltage to another. A campus has large transformers at the substation and many smaller ones next to each building.
whyItExists: Servers run on low-voltage power, but power arrives at high voltage. Each step-down requires a transformer, and redundancy requires spares.
communityImpact: Transformers produce a continuous low-frequency hum that can carry farther than higher-pitched sounds, which is a common source of noise complaints near property lines. They also contain cooling oil that must be managed to protect soil and water.
mitigation: Distance is the main tool (Fairfax County requires major equipment setbacks from homes), plus sound walls, low-noise transformer designs, and oil containment basins required by environmental rules.
monitoring: Property-line acoustic measurements before and after construction, spill prevention plans (SPCC) filed under federal rules, and county noise ordinance enforcement.

name: Server Hall
whatItIs: The large windowless rooms holding rows of computer racks. This is the actual product of the facility: computing, storage, and networking equipment.
whyItExists: Everything else on the campus (power, cooling, security) exists to keep these machines running without interruption.
communityImpact: The building itself is the biggest visual change: warehouse-scale structures that can exceed a million square feet on large campuses. Inside equipment is not audible outside; the community-facing impacts come from the building's size, lighting, and the mechanical systems serving it.
mitigation: Architectural facade standards, height limits, and screening now appear in ordinances in Virginia, Arizona, and Illinois. Landscaped buffers and dark-sky compliant lighting reduce visual impact.
monitoring: Site plans and elevation drawings are public during zoning review, and visual simulations from specific viewpoints can be required before approval.

name: Cooling Plant
whatItIs: The equipment that removes heat from the servers: chillers, cooling towers or dry coolers, pumps, and increasingly liquid loops that carry heat straight off the chips.
whyItExists: Every watt of electricity used by servers becomes heat that must leave the building, or the equipment fails within minutes.
communityImpact: This is where the water and noise questions live. Evaporative designs use large volumes of water but less electricity; dry and closed-loop designs use little or no water but roughly 5 to 15 percent more energy. Fans on rooftop units and cooling towers are a leading noise source.
mitigation: Closed-loop and zero-water-evaporation designs (now standard for some hyperscalers' new builds), reclaimed water where evaporative cooling is used, low-speed fan arrays, and acoustic screening around mechanical yards.
monitoring: Water meters and utility billing records, water use permits, and annual noise studies of the kind Chandler, Arizona requires for five years after construction.

name: Backup Generators
whatItIs: Rows of engine-driven generators, usually diesel, sized to run the entire facility if the grid fails. Each has a fuel tank and an exhaust stack.
whyItExists: Data centers promise near-continuous uptime, and batteries alone cannot carry a full campus through a multi-hour outage.
communityImpact: Generators are mostly idle but must be test-run periodically, producing engine noise and diesel exhaust. Their air permits are often the single largest permitting item, and unpermitted generation (as happened with turbines in Memphis) can become a major community trust issue.
mitigation: Air permits limiting run hours and emissions, scheduled daytime-only testing with resident notification (a Chandler ordinance requirement), Tier 4 emission controls, generator setbacks (300 feet from homes in Fairfax County), and alternatives like fuel cells or batteries for part of the fleet.
monitoring: Air permits and emissions reports are public through the state or county air agency, and test schedules can be published on a community dashboard.

name: Battery Systems (UPS)
whatItIs: Large battery installations that carry the facility for the seconds to minutes between a grid outage and generator start. Some new campuses add much larger grid-scale batteries on site.
whyItExists: Servers cannot tolerate even a momentary power gap, so batteries bridge the transition instantly.
communityImpact: Batteries are quiet and emission-free in operation. The main community question is fire safety: lithium-ion systems require specific firefighting approaches, and fire departments need training and pre-plans before the facility opens.
mitigation: Fire codes (NFPA 855) governing spacing and suppression, thermal runaway detection, coordination and funded training with the local fire department, and safer chemistries (including multi-day iron-air batteries now planned at some campuses).
monitoring: Fire marshal plan review and inspection records, and hazardous materials disclosures filed with local emergency planning committees.

name: Water System
whatItIs: The pipes, tanks, and treatment equipment that supply the cooling plant and manage what leaves the site, including blowdown discharge and stormwater from roofs and pavement.
whyItExists: Facilities using evaporative cooling need reliable water supply, and every facility needs to manage stormwater and any discharge legally.
communityImpact: Depending on design, water use ranges from about what a large office building uses (per Virginia's legislative audit) to hundreds of millions of gallons a year for large evaporative campuses in hot climates. Discharge quality and stormwater runoff affect local streams.
mitigation: Closed-loop or waterless cooling designs, reclaimed or non-potable supply lines, discharge permits with tested limits, and on-site stormwater detention required by modern site plans.
monitoring: Utility water billing, withdrawal and discharge permits, and public reporting: some jurisdictions now require water use estimates during rezoning so commitments are on the record.

name: Security & Lighting
whatItIs: Perimeter fencing, gates, cameras, lighting, and staffed checkpoints controlling who enters the campus.
whyItExists: The facility holds valuable equipment and sensitive data, and uptime contracts require strict physical access control.
communityImpact: Fencing and lighting change the look and feel of the site edge, and poorly aimed lighting causes glare and night-sky impacts for neighbors. Security requirements are also why the public cannot freely tour operating facilities, which can feed distrust.
mitigation: Dark-sky compliant, downward-shielded fixtures (lighting standards now appear in Loudoun County requirements), decorative fencing and berms instead of bare chain link, and scheduled community tours or digital tours as a transparency substitute.
monitoring: Photometric lighting plans submitted during site plan review, and complaint response commitments through a named community liaison.

name: Network / Fiber
whatItIs: The fiber optic lines connecting the campus to the internet, usually buried in conduit along road rights-of-way, plus the meet-me rooms where carriers interconnect.
whyItExists: A data center is only useful if data can flow in and out at enormous volume, so multiple redundant fiber routes are essential.
communityImpact: Short-term street and shoulder disruption while fiber is trenched, and then almost nothing visible in operation. The positive side: fiber routes built for a data center can improve regional broadband options, and hyperscale sites measurably grow local telecom employment.
mitigation: Boring instead of open trenching in sensitive areas, coordinated joint-trench construction to avoid repeat digs, and agreements to extend broadband access to underserved areas as a community benefit.
monitoring: Right-of-way permits from the county or city, construction schedules published in advance, and any broadband commitments written into development agreements.
